rows.evidence: Q1: Sec 2 Methodology - 10 pilot household farms given drip kits and hand-dug wells, 50 non-pilot farms as control, yield and water productivity measured, plus questionnaires and focus groups. Q2: Sec 3.4, Figs 9-10 - drip intervention increased yields by 56-120% for all crops except maize compared with traditional surface irrigation. Q3: Sec 3.4 yield measurement plus Sec 3.5 interviews/focus groups in which farmers reported the system improves their crop yields (measurement and farmer survey). Q6: Sec 2 and 3.4 - effect reported across 10 household farms in three kebeles of Haramaya District, i.e. at farm/kebele level rather than a single plot. Q7: Sec 4 Conclusions - authors state that financial and technical support, capacity building and market access are needed for efficient use of the drip systems and improvement of yields; Sec 2 notes on-farm training was required as drip was new to farmers. Q8: Sec 4 - study states limitations: socio-economic and biophysical factors (soil type and depth, nutrients, landscape, rainfall) not considered; Sec 3.4 - yields measured only once a year out of two seasons.
rows.notes: Intervention bundles drip irrigation with private hand-dug wells, so the yield effect cannot be attributed to drip alone. Study crops are potatoes, carrots, garlic, onions, cabbage and maize; tomato (named in the passage) is not among the crops reported. Q4: water availability and 65% uniform distribution are asserted without a described measurement, so no intermediate variable is credibly measured. Q5: three kebeles were chosen for different climate/hydrology but yield results are not reported separately per kebele. Q9: the 56-120% figure is a spread across crops, not a dispersion measure; no SD, SE or CI reported. Q3 answered yes with some doubt since the farmer-survey evidence on yield is a brief perception statement.

notes: Text appears complete apart from figures/tables not reproduced; small sample (10 intervention farms) and no statistical testing reported.
